title: Chapter 45: The Allure 3
content:
Chapter 45

For reasons he couldn't quite name, Wei Wuxian woke up with a vague, gnawing sense of guilt. He hadn't dared crawl onto the daybed to squeeze in beside Lan Wangji like he usually did, opting instead to rough it on the floorboards for the night. Sometime before dawn, his head had lolled sideways against the wooden frame, and he’d drifted off. Shifting half-conscious in the early morning chill, he felt a pair of gentle hands scoop him up and lay him flat across the mattress. Cracking an eye open with great effort, Lan Wangji’s characteristically frosty face filled his view.

That knocked the cobwebs out of his head real fast. "Lan Zhan," he called out softly.

Lan Wangji hummed a quiet“Mm”in acknowledgment.

"Are you sober right now, or still sleeping it off?"

"Sober."

Wei Wuxian exhaled. "Right... five in the morning, then."

Lan Wangji’s internal clock was ridiculously punctual; the man woke at the hour of the Rabbit every single day without fail, meaning Wei Wuxian didn't even need to check the window to know the time. Lan Wangji reached out and took his wrists. Both were ringed with angry, raw red chafing marks. Pulling a small celadon jar from his sleeve, he bent his head to dab on an ointment. The velvety salve sent a soothing chill through the burning scrapes, making Wei Wuxian squint in relief. "Ow, that smarts... Honestly, Hanguang-jun, you have terrible manners when you're drunk."

Lan Wangji didn't even look up. "You reap what you sow."

Wei Wuxian’s heart did a nervous little hop. "Lan Zhan... you really don't remember anything you did while plastered, right?"

"I do not."

Whew. He definitely doesn't,Wei Wuxian thought.If he did, he'd have skinned me alive out of sheer mortification by now.

Part of him was wildly relieved Lan Wangji had drawn a blank, but another, pettier part found it a bit of a shame. It felt like sneaking a bite of forbidden candy in secret—tucked away in a dark corner, grinning to himself because he’d gotten away with it, but secretly wishing he could boast about the illicit thrill. His gaze drifted downward on pure instinct, zeroing in on Lan Wangji’s lips.

The man never smiled, but those lips looked incredibly soft. And in fact, theyweresoft.

Wei Wuxian caught himself unconsciously nibbling his own bottom lip, his mind instantly wandering off the deep end:The Gusu Lan Clan is so painfully uptight, and Lan Zhan is as dense as a brick when it comes to romance. He’s definitely never kissed a girl before. What do I do now? I went and stole his first kiss! Should I tell him? Would he cry from sheer outrage? Well, little teenage Lan Zhan might’ve thrown a tantrum, but grown-up Hanguang-jun probably won't. Besides, he lives like an ascetic monk; he probably never even had those kinds of urges to begin with... Wait, hold on! Last time he got drunk, I asked him if he had someone he liked, and he point-blank said "Yes." What if he already kissed them ages ago? Then again, knowing how rigidly repressed Lan Zhan is, he definitely strictly adheres to decorum. He probably hasn't kissed anyone—hell, he probably hasn't even held their hand! Come to think of it, maybe he didn't even understand what kind of "like" I was asking about...

Just as Lan Wangji finished applying the ointment, three polite, rhythmic knocks tapped against the door. Lan Sizhui’s voice floated through the wood: "Hanguang-jun, everyone is up. Are we ready to depart?"

"Wait downstairs," Lan Wangji replied.

Once the party cleared the town gates, it was time for the group to part ways. Originally, these young masters had merely been passing acquaintances, casually nodding at one another during the great sects' discussion conferences. But over the past few days, they’d tracked slaughtered cats together, survived a harrowing night in a foggy ghost town, burned roadside paper offerings, snuck illicit sips of wine, picked fights, and traded insults side by side. By now, they were thick as thieves. Parting was agonizingly slow; they dawdled by the stone archway, trading eager promises about when to visit whose estate for summer banquets, or whose territory to crash for upcoming night-hunts.

Lan Wangji didn't rush them, letting them chatter away while he waited beneath the shade of an old tree. Fairy, thoroughly pinned beneath Hanguang-jun's icy glare, didn't dare bark or run wild, curling meekly by the roots while staring longingly toward Jin Ling, tail wagging like a blur.

Taking advantage of Lan Wangji keeping the hound locked down, Wei Wuxian slung an arm around Jin Ling’s shoulders and steered him a healthy distance away.

Mo Xuanyu was one of Jin Guangshan's illegitimate sons—a half-brother to both Jin Zixuan and Jin Guangyao. Genetically speaking, he was technically Jin Ling's uncle, giving him full license to pull rank and lecture the boy like an elder. He strolled along, advising, "When you get back, stop picking fights with your uncle and biting his head off. Do what he says, watch your back, and stop running off on solo night-hunts by yourself."

Jin Ling was born with a golden spoon, but nasty gossip never spared anyone. Growing up an orphan, it was only natural he was desperate to prove himself, eager to chase quick glory. Wei Wuxian softened his tone: "You're only a teenager. Cultivators your age haven't bagged any earth-shattering beasts yet—why rush into the fire just to snatch first place?"

Jin Ling muttered sullenly, "My uncle and my youngest uncle made their names when they were teenagers."

As if that's the same thing!Wei Wuxian thought.Back then, the Qishan Wen Clan was breathing down everyone's necks. Panic was in the air; if you didn't train like a demon and fight for your life, you didn't know if you'd be the next corpse in a ditch. During the Sunshot Campaign, they dragged boys onto the frontlines regardless of whether you were sixteen or sixty. These days, the world is peaceful and the clans are stable; the pressure's off, so naturally nobody trains like a maniac anymore. There's simply no need for it.

Jin Ling pressed on, "Even that dog Wei Ying was barely a teenager when he slayed the Tortoise of Slaughter. If he could do it, why can't I?"

Hearing his own name welded to that lovely epithet sent a violent shudder through Wei Wuxian’s spine. Shaking off the goosebumps, he scoffed, "Did he actually kill it? Wasn't it Hanguang-jun who brought it down?"

Hearing Lan Wangji brought up, Jin Ling cast a deeply suspicious side-eye at him. He hesitated, biting his tongue before huffing, "You and Hanguang-jun... whatever. That's your private business. I couldn't care less. If you want to be a cutsleeve, go right ahead—it's not like that disease is curable anyway."

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "How on earth is that a disease?" Internally, he was dying of laughter:The kid actually thinks I'm shamelessly chasing Lan Zhan!

Jin Ling continued, "I already found out what the Gusu Lan forehead ribbon means. Since things have already come to this, you'd better behave yourself and stick by Hanguang-jun's side. Even cutsleeves should have some self-respect—stop flirting with other men, especially anyone from my family! Otherwise, don't blame me if I get nasty."

By "my family," he clearly meant both the Lanling Jin and Yunmeng Jiang clans. It seemed his tolerance for homosexuals had expanded a fraction: as long as you didn't hit on his relatives, he’d look the other way.

Wei Wuxian sputtered, "You little brat! What do you mean 'flirting with other men'? You make me sound like a total wanton! And what's this about the ribbon? Does the Gusu Lan forehead ribbon actually mean something?"

Jin Ling sneered. "Cut the act! Feigning innocence after getting what you wanted—don't get too smug. I'm done talking about this. Tell me the truth: are you Wei Ying?"

Right at the end of his rant, he dropped the hammer out of nowhere—a direct, vicious jab aimed straight for the throat.

Wei Wuxian parried smoothly without missing a beat: "Do you think I look like him?"

Jin Ling stared at him in heavy silence, then suddenly whistled a sharp note. "Fairy!"

Hearing his name called, the hound's tongue lolled as he bounded forward on all fours. Wei Wuxian bolted like his tail was on fire: "We were talking civilly, why the hell are you sicking the dog on me?!"

"Hmph!" Jin Ling yelled after him. "Good riddance!"

With that parting shot, the boy strutted off with his chin high toward Lanling, clearly still terrified of heading back to Lotus Pier to face Jiang Cheng's wrath. The other young masters peeled off in scattered groups, heading for their respective sect gates, until only Wei Wuxian, Lan Wangji, and the small cluster of Lan disciples remained.

As they walked, the juniors couldn't help glancing back over their shoulders every few steps. Lan Jingyi kept his mouth shut, but his crestfallen face was practically screaming his reluctance to part. "Where are we heading next?" he asked.

Lan Sizhui offered, "Ze-wu-jun is currently night-hunting near Tanzhou. Should we head straight back to Cloud Recesses, or link up with him there?"

Lan Wangji answered concisely: "Tanzhou. Rendezvous."

"Sounds like a plan," Wei Wuxian chimed in. "Maybe we can lend a hand. Not like we have a clue where our headless buddy's skull rolled off to anyway."

The two elders walked ahead while the juniors trailed at a respectful distance. After walking a while, Lan Wangji spoke quietly: "Jiang Cheng knows who you are."

Swaying atop the patched donkey while Little Apple ambled along at a crawl, Wei Wuxian sighed. "Yeah, he knows. But so what if he knows? He doesn't have a shred of proof."

A sacrificial summoning wasn't like body-snatching; it left behind no spiritual tracks. Jiang Cheng had solely guessed his identity based on his dead-giveaway reaction to the dog. But first off, Jiang Cheng had never told a living soul about Wei Wuxian's crippling fear of dogs; secondly, subtle body language and panic weren't things an outsider could rely on for ironclad evidence. Even if Jiang Cheng plastered wanted posters across every town square screaming that the terrifying Yiling Laozu turned into a weeping mess at the sight of a puppy, the cultivation world would just assume the Sandu Shengshou had finally lost his marbles after thirteen years of hunting shadows and torturing the wrong suspects.

Wei Wuxian leaned forward. "Which brings me back to my burning question: how on earth didyouspot me?"

Lan Wangji’s voice was dry as bone. "I, too, am deeply curious... as to why your memory is so appalling."

A few days later, before they could meet up with Lan Xichen in Tanzhou, the group passed an enormous walled garden. Seeing how grand and sprawling the grounds were, completely unattended, the juniors couldn't resist their curiosity and slipped inside to explore. So long as their antics didn't violate the sect rules, Lan Wangji never interfered, letting them wander freely.

Stone pavilions, winding balustrades, and weathered tables sat scattered through the foliage, designed for moonlit poetry and flower-viewing. Yet years of wind and rain had taken their toll: the pavilion roof was missing a corner, and a couple of stone benches lay overturned in the dirt. Instead of vibrant blossoms, the grounds were choked with withered brambles and rotting leaves. The estate had clearly been abandoned for ages.

After roaming through the courtyard, Lan Sizhui paused. "This... is the Garden of the Flower-Planting Maiden, isn't it?"

Lan Jingyi blinked. "The who? Does this place have an owner? It looks completely derelict, like nobody's touched it in decades."

Blossoms that bloom in their fleeting, designated season were known asshihua—seasonal flowers. Bursting in endless varieties and colors, their peak filled the air with intoxicating perfume. Hearing the moniker, something clicked in Wei Wuxian's memory.

Sizhui ran a hand over the pavilion's stone pillar, murmuring thoughtfully, "If I recall correctly, it must be. This garden was once quite famous; I read about it in a text. The chapter on theFlower-Planting Maiden's Soulrecorded:'In Tanzhou lies a garden, and in the garden dwells a maiden. Recite poetry beneath the moon; if the verse is sublime, she gifts a seasonal bloom that will not wither for three years, its fragrance ever-lasting. If the verse is clumsy or recited with errors, the maiden appears in a flash, hurls blossoms at the speaker's face, and vanishes.'"

Jingyi gasped, "She pelts you with flowers if you mess up a poem?! I hope they don't have thorns, or my face would be bleeding within two lines! What kind of monster is she?"

"Hardly a monster," Sizhui explained. "A spirit, rather. Legend has it the original master of the grounds was a wandering poet. He planted every blossom with his own hands, treating the flowers as his dearest companions, reciting verses among the petals daily. Steeped in poetic sentiment, the garden's blossoms coalesced into a spiritual entity—the Flower-Planting Maiden. When travelers recited beautiful verse, reminding her of the poet who raised her, she’d joyfully bestow a magical bloom. But if someone mangled the lines, she’d burst from the thicket and slap them silly with a bouquet. The blows would knock them out cold, and they’d wake up dumped outside the perimeter walls. Over a decade ago, visitors lined up day and night just to catch a glimpse of this garden."

Wei Wuxian grinned. "Poetic, truly poetic. Though I know for a fact the Cloud Recesses' Library doesn't stock books on such frivolous folklore. Come clean, Sizhui—what illicit novels have you been flipping through, and who smuggled them to you?"

Sizhui’s ears flushed pink. He stole a nervous, sideways peek at Lan Wangji, terrified of catching a disciplinary lecture.

Jingyi chimed in, "Was she drop-dead gorgeous? Why else would crowds swamp the place?"

Seeing no anger gathering on Lan Wangji's brow, Sizhui breathed a sigh of relief and smiled. "She was said to be remarkably fair. After all, she was an ethereal spirit born of art and nature. But in truth, practically no one ever caught a clear look at her face. Even if a traveler couldn't compose verse on the spot, memorizing a famous stanza or two was child's play, so most walked away with a flower. And the clumsy few who butchered their recitations were knocked unconscious instantly, missing their chance. Well... except for one man."

Another boy piped up, "Who?"

Wei Wuxian cleared his throat lightly.

Sizhui answered, "The Yiling Laozu, Wei Wuxian."

Wei Wuxian coughed again, louder this time. "Ahem. Why does his name keep popping up? Can't we chat about something else?"

Nobody paid him the slightest mind. Lan Jingyi waved him off, worried. "Quiet, you! What did Wei Wuxian do? That great fiend—what did he pull this time? Did he rip the poor maiden out of the garden by force?!"

"Not quite," Sizhui chuckled. "Rather, desperate to get a good look at her face, he journeyed all the way from Yunmeng to Tanzhou specifically to visit this garden. Every single time he stood before the grove, he deliberately mangled his poetry, infuriating the maiden into pelting him with flowers and dumping him outside the walls. The second he woke up, he’d scramble back over the fence and shout wrong verses at the top of his lungs again. He repeated this routine over twenty times until he finally mapped every feature of her face, then spent the next month bragging about her beauty to anyone who would listen. The poor maiden was so thoroughly traumatized by his antics that she refused to show herself for a very long time; the moment he stepped foot inside, she’d unleash a torrential hailstorm of flying blossoms, whipping him bloody. It was quite the spectacle..."

The disciples burst into boisterous laughter. "Wei Wuxian really was the worst!"

"How could anyone be that childish?!"

Wei Wuxian rubbed his nose, grumbling defensively, "What's so childish about that?! Who hasn't pulled a ridiculous stunt or two in their youth? Besides, why does everyone know about that anyway? Recording that sort of gossip in a formal book—that'sthe real definition of having too much time on your hands."

Lan Wangji looked at him. His expression was deadpan as ever, but a subtle, teasing light danced behind his glassy amber eyes, clearly laughing at him.

Wei Wuxian glared back playfully:Oh, look at you, enjoying my embarrassment! I know at least a dozen of your embarrassing teenage secrets, Lan Zhan—just you wait, one of these days I'm spilling the beans to your precious juniors and shattering their pristine image of the untouchable Hanguang-jun!

Turning back to the disciples, Wei Wuxian pointed an accusatory finger: "Look at you lot—distracted and frivolous! You're clearly spending your study hours slacking off on trashy novels instead of practicing your cultivation. When we get back, I'm having Hanguang-jun sentence you to copy the clan rules ten times over."

The boys blanched in sheer horror. "Ten times... while doing handstands?!"

Wei Wuxian froze, whipping around to stare at Lan Wangji. "You make them copy rules while doinghandstands?! That's barbaric!"

Lan Wangji’s voice was calm and even. "Merely copying text fails to instill the lesson in certain individuals. Doing so inverted sharpens the memory and tempers the core."

Wei Wuxian, the undisputed poster child for "failing to learn his lesson," wisely pretended not to catch the subtext, internally praising the heavens that he’d never been subjected to inverted calligraphy in his youth.

The ghost stories had stoked the juniors' enthusiasm, and they collectively decided to camp out in the overgrown garden for the night. Camping in the wild was standard fare for night-hunts anyway, so the boys busied themselves sweeping up dry twigs and dead leaves to build a crackling bonfire. Lan Wangji slipped out to scout the perimeter, ensuring the area was secure while laying down defensive wards to prevent midnight ambushes.

Stretching his legs out by the fire, Wei Wuxian seized the chance now that Lan Wangji was out of earshot. "By the way, quick question for you all: what does your clan's forehead ribbon actually signify?"

The second the words left his mouth, the atmosphere around the fire dropped into awkward silence. The disciples fidgeted, trading stammering glances.

Wei Wuxian’s gut clenched, a sudden thump of anxiety hammering against his ribs.

Lan Sizhui asked hesitantly, "Senior... you genuinely do not know?"

Wei Wuxian rolled his eyes. "Would I be asking if I knew? Do I look like someone who has that much free time?"

Lan Jingyi grumbled under his breath, "Honestly, yeah... You're the guy who tricked us into lining up to gawk through a window crack..."

Wei Wuxian poked a stick into the embers, sending sparks dancing into the dark. "That was to build your character and shatter your limits! It was educational, and mark my words, you'll thank me for it down the road."

Sizhui seemed to carefully weigh his phrasing, hesitating for several long seconds before speaking softly: "It is like this: the Gusu Lan forehead ribbon symbolizes 'self-restraint.' Surely Senior knows this much?"

"I know that part. And?"

Sizhui continued, "Our founding ancestor, Lan An, once decreed: only in the presence of one's fated partner—the one who holds your heart—may all restraint be cast aside. Therefore, the ancestral precept passed down through generations is... well, our clan ribbon is an exceptionally private, deeply sacred belonging. Aside from oneself, no outsider is ever permitted to touch it, let alone untie it, and tying it around another person is an absolute taboo. Unless... unless..."

Unless you were betrothed.

The crackling fire illuminated a circle of flushed, bashful teenage faces, leaving Sizhui too mortified to finish the sentence.

Every drop of blood in Wei Wuxian’s body rushed straight to his face.

The ribbon... that ribbon... holy hell—

The meaning behind that damn ribbon is monstrously heavy!

A sudden, suffocating wave of panic hit him; he desperately needed air. Scrambling to his feet, he practically bolted into the dark, steadying his spinning head against the trunk of a dead tree.

...Gods above! What on earth did I do back then?!

Years ago in Qishan, the Wen Clan had hosted a grand Discussion Conference spanning seven days, featuring a different competitive sport each morning. One of those days had been dedicated to archery.

The rules dictated that unwed disciples who had yet to come of age would enter the hunting grounds to compete. Scattered across the forest were over a thousand life-sized, fast-moving paper targets, but only a hundred were possessed by fierce spirits. Striking a single plain target meant immediate disqualification; only those who continually pierced the possessed paper effigies could remain on the field, with the final rankings tallying who scored the highest and most accurate hits.

Naturally, Wei Wuxian had entered the fray as a frontline competitor for the Yunmeng Jiang Clan. Before the match, he’d sat through hours of tedious sectarian debates, numbing his skull until hoisting his bow and quiver finally injected some life back into his veins.

Yawning as he made his way toward the range gates, his casual sweep caught sight of a frosty, impeccably handsome youth standing nearby. The boy wore a brilliant scarlet round-collared robe cinched with a nine-ring sash, his sleeves bound tight in an archer's cut. It was the standard tournament uniform issued by the Qishan Wen Clan, but on this particular youth, it looked breathtaking—three parts scholarly grace, three parts martial valor, completely eclipsing the field in sheer, blinding elegance.

The youth carried a quiver of snow-white fletched arrows, head bowed as he tested his bowstring. His slender fingers plucked the cord, producing a deep, resonant twang that hummed with the rich timbre of zither strings—melodic, yet brimming with steel.

Wei Wuxian thought he looked familiar. A second later, he slapped his thigh, calling out with boisterous cheer: "Hey! Isn't that Wangji-xiong?!"

By that point, over a year had passed since Wei Wuxian’s three-month boarding stint in Cloud Recesses ended with him being shipped back to Yunmeng in disgrace. Back home, he’d regaled his peers with colorful tales of Gusu—including endless rants about how Lan Wangji’s face was undeniably gorgeous, yet the guy was an uptight, soul-crushing bore—before tossing the memories aside to go back to swimming lakes and hunting pheasants. He’d only ever seen Lan Wangji draped in the Lan Clan's pristine, mourning-white robes; seeing him wrapped in such vibrant, eye-catching scarlet against that ridiculously pretty face had briefly blinded him, taking an extra beat to connect the dots.

Lan Wangji finished testing his bow, turned on his heel, and walked away.

Rebuffed, Wei Wuxian nudged Jiang Cheng. "Ignored me again. Tsk."

Jiang Cheng leveled a deadpan glare at him, refusing to take the bait. The range featured over twenty separate entrances for the respective sects; as Lan Wangji approached the Gusu Lan archway, Wei Wuxian darted ahead to cut him off. Lan Wangji sidestepped left; Wei Wuxian slid left. Lan Wangji stepped right; Wei Wuxian shifted right. A total, deliberate roadblock.

Finally, Lan Wangji halted, lifting his chin with rigid propriety. "Pardon me."

Wei Wuxian grinned. "Oh, so you do speak? Were you pretending not to know me just now, or pretending to be deaf?"

Nearby, disciples from other clans were gawking at the circus, snickering and whispering. Jiang Cheng clicked his tongue in disgust and hoisted his bow, marching off to an entirely different gate.

Lan Wangji’s pale gaze iced over as he repeated, "Pardon me."

Smirking, Wei Wuxian arched a brow and stepped aside. The archway was cramped, forcing Lan Wangji to brush intimately past his chest to cross the threshold.

As the white ribbon fluttered into the ring, Wei Wuxian called after his back, "Lan Zhan, your forehead ribbon is crooked!"

Noble disciples guarded their appearance fiercely—especially the Gusu Lan Clan. Without thinking, Lan Wangji reached up to adjust it, only to find the silk sitting completely straight. He whipped around, glaring daggers at Wei Wuxian, who was already howling with laughter as he jogged toward the Yunmeng Jiang gate.

Once the horn sounded and the hunt officially began, disciples were eliminated in steady droves for clipping normal paper targets. Wei Wuxian picked his targets with lazy precision—shooting slow, but never missing—emptying nearly eighteen arrows from his quiver in no time at all. Just as he was contemplating whether to spice things up by shooting off-hand, something soft brushed against his cheek.

It was gossamer-light, tickling his skin like drifting silk. Turning around, he found that Lan Wangji had drifted close, drawing a full bow at an effigy with his back turned to him.

The long trailing tail of his white ribbon was dancing in the wind, lightly brushing against Wei Wuxian’s cheek.

Wei Wuxian squinted playfully. "Wangji-xiong!"

Lan Wangji drew the bow into a perfect crescent, pausing for a fraction of a second before clipping out, "What."

"Your ribbon is crooked."

Burned once, Lan Wangji wasn't falling for the trick again. Releasing the arrow with a sharp twang, he spat a single word without looking back: "Frivolous."

"I'm serious this time! It really is crooked—look, let me fix it for you!"

True to his impulsive nature, his hand moved before his brain caught up, snagging the fluttering tail of the ribbon floating before his eyes. But Wei Wuxian suffered from a chronic habit of fidgeting; having grown up tugging on the pigtails of Yunmeng maidens, the moment his fingers curled around a dangling ribbon, muscle memory took over and gave it a mischievous yank.

To his horror, the ribbon had already been slightly loose; under his tug, the silk slid cleanly off Lan Wangji’s brow.

The hand gripping Lan Wangji’s bow gave a violent tremor.

A painfully long silence hung in the air before he turned around—moving with agonizing, rigid slowness—his gaze locking onto Wei Wuxian.

Wei Wuxian stood there, holding the soft white silk in his palm, stammering awkwardly: "My bad... I didn't mean to. Here, you can tie it back on."

Lan Wangji’s face was an absolute catastrophe.

Dark, suffocating wrath practically radiated from his brow, veins bulging across the hand white-knuckling his bow, his entire frame shaking with raw fury. Spotting the faint crimson veins creeping into his pale eyes, Wei Wuxian nervously squished the ribbon in his fist, thinking in panic:I only pulled a piece of cloth off, right? It’s not like I ripped off an arm!

Seeing the shameless rogue dare to crumple his ribbon, Lan Wangji lunged and snatched the silk from his grip.

Wei Wuxian let go immediately. The remaining Lan disciples ceased shooting, swarming the scene in a protective huddle. Lan Xichen wrapped an arm around his brother’s trembling shoulders, whispering urgent consolations to the dead-silent Lan Wangji, while the other Lan disciples stood rigid as stone, throwing horrified, deeply bizarre looks at Wei Wuxian.

Wei Wuxian could only catch scattered fragments of their hushed murmurs:"An accident..." "No need for anger..." "Pay it no mind..." "A man..." "The clan rules..."He stood there, sinking deeper into total bewilderment.

Lan Wangji leveled one final, murderous glare at him, snapped his sleeves, and marched straight off the field, forfeiting the match on the spot.

Jiang Cheng strolled over, scowling. "What did you pull this time? Didn't I tell you to stop provoking him? If you don't court death once a day, you can't sleep at night, can you?"

Wei Wuxian threw his hands up. "I told him his ribbon was crooked! The first time was a joke, but the second time was the truth! He didn't believe me and threw a fit. I didn't pull it off on purpose—why is he acting like I killed his dog? He even quit the tournament!"

Jiang Cheng scoffed, "Isn't it obvious? Because you are exceptionally repulsive to him!"

Seeing Jiang Cheng’s quiver was nearly empty, Wei Wuxian had shoved the drama to the back of his mind and focused on the hunt.

For over a decade, he had never spared that afternoon another thought. He’d vaguely wondered if the ribbon carried some quirky family lore, but once the competition wrapped up, he’d forgotten all about it.

Now, recalling the shell-shocked stares of the Lan disciples that day...

In broad daylight, in front of the entire cultivation world, he had publicly stripped the sacred forehead ribbon from the Second Young Master Lan—and Lan Wangji hadn't shot him dead on the spot! The man's self-restraint was truly terrifying! A living saint!

And worse... looking back over the past few weeks, he had laid his sticky fingers on that ribbon more than once!

Back by the bonfire, Lan Jingyi scratched his head, watching the silhouette pacing in the dark. "What is he doing pacing around like that? Did he eat too much and can't sit still?"

Another disciple chimed in, "His face keeps flashing red, then white... Did he eat something bad?"

"We all ate the same rations... Is it because of the ribbon's meaning? He doesn't need to get this hysterical about it. Guess he really is hopelessly infatuated with Hanguang-jun—look at him, practically jumping for joy..."

Wei Wuxian had looped around a cluster of dead brambles fifty times before finally regaining a sliver of sanity, almost choking on his own spit at that parting remark.

Right then, the crisp crunch of dry leaves snapping broke from the trees behind him.

The heavy, steady tread didn't sound like a child—Lan Wangji was likely back from his patrol. Wei Wuxian smoothed his expression into a neutral mask and spun around on his heel.

Standing in the long shadows cast by a withered elm tree was a tall, dark silhouette.

The figure was towering, broad-shouldered, and radiated an oppressive, suffocating aura of martial dominance.

The only thing missing was its head.
